headline: Warm, dry Santa Ana weather lasts through Friday, then the pattern flips to cool and wet next week, led by a strong storm that could start as early as Monday night or Tuesday morning with 1 to 3 inches of rain on the coast, 3 to 5 inches in the mountains and possible thunderstorms.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Thanksgiving is another classic warm, dry Southern California day around Glendale and across the region, with Santa Ana (northeast offshore) winds keeping humidity at just 15 to 25 percent. A Wind Advisory runs until 2 PM this afternoon for some areas and another until 9 AM Friday for others. Tonight stays dry, with only light north to northeast breezes at LAX at times.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Friday is just as warm, with highs peaking in the upper 70s to mid 80s before the offshore winds start to weaken; some gusty winds return but are weaker and mostly limited to the Santa Susana and Santa Lucia ranges. It stays dry through Saturday, with cooling beginning over the weekend. A very weak first storm Sunday afternoon into Monday morning may not even bring measurable rain everywhere, with at most about a tenth of an inch.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: The storm door is open next week, with at least two more storms. The second, much stronger storm now looks about 12 hours sooner, with rain starting as early as Monday night or Tuesday morning; it carries unusually high moisture for a winter storm, and models agree well on a high chance of heavy rain, roughly 1 to 3 inches on the coast and 3 to 5 inches in the mountains. Thunderstorms are a good possibility, severe weather is possible, and some long-range guidance shows winds over 50 mph at the storm's peak, so people near areas burned in the last year or two should watch the forecast closely. A third, much weaker storm is expected later in the week.

coast: A large, long-period west swell combined with exceptionally high tides brought large surf and moderate to significant coastal flooding this morning, worst on the Central Coast from Point Conception northward, the Ventura County coast and far eastern parts of the southern Santa Barbara County coast; elsewhere impacts are a bit less but still concerning, and much above normal tides continue into Friday morning, when the morning high tide is the time of greatest concern for low-lying, unprotected spots. Coastal Flood Advisories run until noon Friday, 3 PM Friday or 2 PM Saturday, and High Surf Advisories until 9 PM tonight, 3 PM Saturday or 9 PM Saturday, depending on the stretch of coast, with a Beach Hazards Statement through Saturday afternoon for other beaches. Expect strong rip currents nearly everywhere, strong along-shore currents, sneaker waves, heavy shore break, coastal erosion and a higher risk of damage to coastal structures, making swimming dangerous. On the water, large breaking waves near the coast and harbor entrances can capsize small boats today; Small Craft Advisories run until 3 PM today, 3 AM Friday or 3 AM Saturday depending on the area, with offshore winds near shore from Point Mugu to Santa Monica this afternoon and rough seas on the outer waters and north of Point Sal through Friday night. Conditions are mostly calmer Saturday through Monday, then winds rise to advisory levels or higher Monday night ahead of the strong midweek storm.
watch_for: Timing and strength of the strong midweek storm, which now could start as early as Monday night or Tuesday morning
Heavy rain, possible thunderstorms and 50+ mph gusts near recent burn areas
Coastal flooding at Friday morning's high tide in low-lying, unprotected spots
confidence: Forecasters are highly confident in the warm, dry weather through Saturday, see good model agreement on a strong midweek storm with a high chance of heavy rain while cautioning that its timing and strength can still shift 4 to 5 days out, and have moderate to high confidence in the marine forecast.
